author: Breana Sinclair
title: City Council votes to revert 4th and 5th Street back to pre-pilot design - NewsBreak
text: GRAND JUNCTION, Colo. ( KREX ) — During the Grand Junction City Council meeting on Wednesday, Council members discussed a resolution to revert portions of 4th and 5th due to monetary concerns of moving forward with the project. The resolution passed with a 4-3 vote. On May 29, the Council unanimously voted to move forward with the option to add a two-lane bike lane for the 4th and 5th Street Improvements Pilot Project. Revisions to the project were made to provide the additional asphalt width required for improvements to the existing infrastructure. During a work session on Aug. 4, the City Council reviewed the proposed changes, project costs and schedules. With a primary concern regarding the estimated $250,000 cost to implement the changes, the Council was advised to return with a formal request to authorize reverting both corridors from Grand Avenue and Ute Avenue to their pre-pilot design. With the passed resolution to revert portions of the corridors to their pre-pilot designs, work to open up entry and exit ways from 4th and 5th Streets to the Colorado Avenue parking lots and replace parking meters alongside the two streets is estimated to start on Sept. 2 and take approximately three weeks to complete. During the Wednesday meeting, dozens of community members spoke about the decision to revert the pilot project, with varied and ranged reactions to the topic. Some individuals were upset that the pilot was implemented in the first place, citing concerns such as loss of small business revenues, their experience of not seeing bikers on 4th or 5th Street and the changes being more dangerous. Others were upset that the decision to reverse the project was on the table, arguing that the changes were safer and adaptive to the community. A few people thought that the City Council should work on creating a different compromise, sharing their frustration with going against the original recommendations of officials, which has wasted the time of community members and officials. After public comment, the City Council asked questions and shared their thoughts. Council members Scott Beilfuss and Anna Stout agreed that the 2.0 version of the pilot was a good compromise and a better option. Both thought that the Council’s handling of the project did not build trust with the community and created unnecessary drama. Beilfuss pointed out that he thought the resolution’s wording was fussy and did not make it clear exactly what the council was voting on. Council member Laurel Cole commented that whatever decision is made, safety points need to be addressed, and shared a sentiment with Stout and some community members that the Council had other areas to focus its time on besides the 4th and 5th Street Project. Council member Robert Ballard commented that he had made compromises with the project that he did not personally like, so now it was time for the other side to make compromises that they did not like. Mayor Cody Kennedy spoke at the end before calling for a vote, mentioning that he was disappointed with the Council’s overall lack of transparency with the project and the unwillingness to compromise.
